summary: Failure modes generated and agreement-checked from 300 traces.

codes.name: Agent_Refusal_Or_Task_Abandonment
codes.description: An agent declines to produce a substantive response or stops engaging with the task mid-execution, resulting in no usable output for the current pipeline stage. This is an agent-level behavioral failure distinct from orchestration-level stage skipping.
codes.when_to_use: When an agent explicitly refuses the task (e.g., safety refusal, capability disclaimer) or silently produces an empty/non-substantive response despite receiving valid input.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the stage is skipped due to routing/orchestration logic rather than agent behavior (use A.7). When output is cut off by a resource limit (use A.4). When the process is killed by infrastructure (use A.5).

codes.name: Instruction_Constraint_Ignored
codes.description: An agent fails to adhere to explicit instructions or constraints provided in its system prompt or task input, producing output that violates one or more stated requirements despite having received them.
codes.when_to_use: When the agent's output demonstrably violates a specific, explicit instruction or constraint present in the input it received — such as format requirements, length limits, content exclusions, or procedural steps.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the instruction was not actually present in the input received by the agent (use A.12 if it was lost in handoff). When the agent explicitly acknowledges and explains why it cannot follow an instruction (use A.1). When the constraint is implicit or ambiguous rather than explicit.

codes.name: Intra_Agent_Self_Contradiction
codes.description: An agent contradicts its own earlier statements or reasoning within a single output, producing internally inconsistent content that cannot be reliably used by downstream stages without manual resolution.
codes.when_to_use: When a single agent's output contains two or more statements, conclusions, or reasoning steps that are mutually exclusive or logically incompatible with each other.
codes.when_not_to_use: When contradictions arise from information loss across pipeline stages (use A.12). When the contradiction is between two different agents' outputs rather than within a single output.

codes.name: Output_Ended_Before_Completion
codes.description: Apply this code when the final state of the agent output shows structural or semantic incompleteness based on what the output itself has already established. Annotators must evaluate only what is physically present in the output — not what the ideal response should have contained. An output is incomplete if it ends while any of the following conditions are true: (1) OPEN STRUCTURES: A bracket, brace, parenthesis, code fence, XML/HTML tag, quote block, or table row was opened and never closed — check by scanning the full output for unmatched delimiters. (2) INTERRUPTED SENTENCE: The last sentence contains a subject and verb but ends without terminal punctuation (period, question mark, exclamation mark, ellipsis) AND the sentence does not form a grammatically complete standalone thought. (3) ABANDONED ENUMERATION: A numbered list, lettered list, or multi-step sequence explicitly states or implies a total count (e.g., 'There are five steps:', 'First...', 'Step 1 of 4') and the output stops before that count is reached. (4) MISSING PROMISED ELEMENT: The output explicitly names or introduces an element it has not yet delivered — for example, 'Here is the summary:', 'The following table shows:', or 'In conclusion,' — and that element is absent or contains zero content. All four criteria must be evaluated by inspecting only the characters present in the output.
codes.when_to_use: Use this code when at least ONE of the four numbered criteria is objectively satisfied by inspecting the output text: (A) you can identify a specific unclosed delimiter or tag by scanning from open to close; (B) the final word or phrase is mid-sentence with no terminal punctuation and cannot stand alone as a complete thought; (C) the output explicitly stated a number of items or steps and you can count that fewer were delivered; (D) a transition phrase that introduces forthcoming content appears but the content that was introduced is absent or empty. The code applies regardless of output length — a short output can be complete and a long output can be incomplete.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do NOT use this code in the following situations: (1) STYLISTIC BREVITY: The output is short or terse but does not violate any of the four criteria — brevity alone is not incompleteness. (2) OMITTED BUT UNPROMISED CONTENT: Content that an annotator believes should have been included but was never signaled by the output itself — apply this code only to content the output explicitly set up. (3) TERMINAL ELLIPSIS BY CONVENTION: The output ends with '...' as a deliberate stylistic or rhetorical device and the surrounding context makes this intent clear. (4) COMPLETE FINAL SENTENCE WITHOUT CLOSING FORMALITY: The output ends with a fully punctuated sentence that forms a complete thought, even if a summary or sign-off might have been a nice addition — the absence of an optional closing does not qualify unless the output itself explicitly promised one. (5) PARTIAL ANSWER TO AN AMBIGUOUS PROMPT: If the prompt was vague and the agent answered one valid interpretation fully, this is not truncation — it is a scoping decision.

codes.name: Execution_Terminated_By_System
codes.description: The agent process is killed, times out, or crashes due to infrastructure-level resource exhaustion (OOM kill signals, CPU hard limits, process watchdog termination) or platform-level errors, resulting in no output or a fatally incomplete response. Distinct from model-level generation truncation (A.4) in that the failure occurs at the process or runtime layer, not within the generation loop.
codes.when_to_use: When the agent invocation fails entirely or produces no output due to a process-level signal (SIGKILL, SIGTERM), out-of-memory kernel kill, hard timeout enforced by an orchestrator, or an unhandled runtime exception that terminates the process.
codes.when_not_to_use: When output is cut off by a model-level token or generation limit rather than a process kill (use A.4). When failure is due to an external API rate limit (use A.6). When the agent voluntarily refuses or abandons the task (use A.1).

codes.name: Rate_Limit_Induced_Failure
codes.description: Agent invocation fails or produces degraded output because an external API or service rate limit or quota was reached, preventing the agent from completing its task. Applies strictly to quota/rate-limit responses from external APIs, not to infrastructure-level process termination.
codes.when_to_use: When the agent fails due to an HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests), quota-exceeded error, or equivalent rate-limit signal from an external API or model provider.
codes.when_not_to_use: When failure is due to process-level resource exhaustion or infrastructure termination (use A.5). When the API returns an error other than a rate limit (e.g., authentication failure, server error). When output is merely slow but eventually completes.

codes.name: Pipeline_Stage_Skipped
codes.description: One stage of the sequential pipeline is bypassed or its output is not produced due to orchestration or routing logic, causing downstream stages to operate on incomplete input or the pipeline to produce no final output. Distinct from agent-level refusal in that the skip is caused by the pipeline's control flow, not by the agent's own behavior.
codes.when_to_use: When a pipeline stage is omitted because of a conditional branch, misconfigured routing rule, failed dependency check, or orchestration error — not because the agent at that stage refused or failed.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the stage produces no output because the agent refused or abandoned the task (use A.1, which may then trigger A.7 as a downstream consequence). When the stage fails due to resource exhaustion or system termination (use A.5).

codes.name: Redundant_Pass_Through_Without_Value
codes.description: A pipeline stage accepts and re-emits a prior stage's output unchanged without adding any verification, correction, improvement, or value, wasting a pipeline stage and providing false assurance that the content was reviewed.
codes.when_to_use: When a stage whose role is to check, refine, or improve prior output produces output that is identical or trivially paraphrased from its input, with no substantive changes, corrections, or additions.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the stage correctly determines no changes are needed and explicitly documents its verification reasoning (deliberate no-change with justification is not a failure). When the stage is intentionally a pass-through by design.

codes.name: Repetitive_Looping_Output
codes.description: An agent produces output containing pathological repetition of content, phrases, sentences, or structural patterns, indicating a generation loop or failure to advance through the response, rendering the output unusable.
codes.when_to_use: When agent output contains the same phrase, sentence, paragraph, or structural block repeated multiple times in a way that is clearly unintentional and degrades output utility.
codes.when_not_to_use: When repetition is intentional and instructed (e.g., a template with repeated sections). When mild stylistic repetition occurs but does not impair the usability of the output.

codes.name: Context_Loss_Across_Pipeline_Handoff
codes.description: A downstream agent or stage produces output that is visibly inconsistent with, ignorant of, or contradictory to information that was explicitly present in an upstream stage's output or the original input. The failure must be attributable to a transmission or capacity problem between stages — not to reasoning errors, misinterpretation, or deliberate summarization. Three observable sub-types qualify: (1) Context window overflow: the downstream agent's input demonstrably omits earlier content because the combined token count of all passed context would exceed the model's known context limit — flag by checking whether the missing information appeared only in early portions of a long upstream output; (2) Incomplete passthrough: a pipeline component (e.g., orchestrator, retriever, formatter) can be identified as having truncated, filtered, or reformatted the upstream output before passing it on, causing specific fields, facts, or instructions to disappear; (3) Format corruption: the upstream output was structurally transformed (e.g., JSON parsed incorrectly, markdown stripped, encoding error) such that semantic content is lost or garbled in transmission. In all cases, annotators must be able to point to (a) a specific piece of information present upstream and (b) evidence that it is absent or wrong downstream.
codes.when_to_use: Use this code when ALL of the following are true: (1) You can identify a specific fact, instruction, constraint, or data item that was present in stage N's output or the original task input; (2) Stage N+1 (or later) acts as if that information does not exist — e.g., repeats a question already answered, ignores a constraint already specified, produces output inconsistent with earlier established facts; (3) The most plausible explanation is a pipeline transmission failure (truncation, overflow, filtering, corruption) rather than a reasoning or interpretation failure. Explicitly annotate which sub-type applies: overflow, incomplete passthrough, or format corruption, and cite the specific missing content as evidence.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do NOT use this code when: (1) The downstream agent received the information but misunderstood or misapplied it — that is a reasoning or instruction-following failure, not a handoff loss; (2) The upstream stage never actually produced the information (the loss originated within that stage, not in transmission); (3) Information was intentionally summarized or condensed by design and the system behaved as expected — planned lossy compression is not a handoff failure; (4) The only evidence is that the final output is wrong, with no traceable link to a specific upstream piece of information going missing between stages; (5) A single-agent, single-stage system is involved — there is no pipeline handoff to fail.

codes.name: Solver_Constraint_Violation_In_Output
codes.description: The solver produces output that directly violates one or more explicit formatting, structural, or content constraints specified in the task (e.g., ignoring a word limit, using a prohibited format, omitting a required section, or including forbidden content).
codes.when_to_use: When the solver's output can be checked against an explicit constraint stated in the prompt and found non-compliant — regardless of whether the underlying answer is otherwise correct.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply when the constraint violation is introduced by the checker during a later editing step (use B.5); do not apply when the solver's output is merely incomplete or wrong in substance but no explicit constraint is broken (use B.2 or B.10).

codes.name: Solver_Incorrect_Or_Logically_Flawed_Solution
codes.description: The solver produces a solution (code, algorithm, answer, computation, or argument) that contains at least one verifiably wrong positive claim or result. A 'positive claim' means the solver asserts something IS the case — a specific value, a factual statement, a logical conclusion, a code output, or a step-by-step result — and that assertion can be checked against ground truth, formal logic, or domain knowledge and found to be incorrect. Examples include: returning the wrong numerical answer, writing code that produces incorrect output when executed, making a factually false statement presented as true, drawing a logically invalid conclusion from premises, or applying a formula/rule incorrectly. The error must be present in what WAS produced, not in what was omitted. If the solution is both wrong AND incomplete, still apply this code.
codes.when_to_use: 1. The solver states a specific fact, value, or result and it is demonstrably false (e.g., claims the capital of Australia is Sydney, computes 12*12=148). 2. The solver's code, when executed or traced, produces an output that contradicts the stated or expected correct output. 3. The solver applies a formula, rule, or theorem incorrectly, leading to a wrong result (e.g., misapplies the quadratic formula). 4. The solver presents a logical argument where a stated conclusion does not follow from the stated premises (internal contradiction or invalid inference). 5. The solution is both wrong and incomplete — this code takes priority over B.10 in that case.
codes.when_not_to_use: 1. The solver's answer is merely incomplete, missing steps, or partially addressed but what IS stated is correct — use B.10 instead. 2. The solver explicitly acknowledges uncertainty or says 'I don't know' without making a wrong positive claim — that is a refusal or limitation, not an incorrect solution. 3. The solver produces a valid alternative solution that differs from an expected answer due to ambiguity in the problem, and the solver's interpretation is reasonable. 4. The error is purely stylistic, formatting-related, or a minor typo that does not change the correctness of the substantive answer. 5. The solver's approach is suboptimal or inefficient but still produces a correct result — inefficiency alone is not an error.

codes.name: Solver_Inappropriate_Approach_Or_Method
codes.description: The solver uses a method, algorithm, strategy, or tool that is fundamentally inappropriate for the problem — either explicitly prohibited by the task or clearly unsuitable given the problem's requirements — even if the approach might yield a superficially plausible output.
codes.when_to_use: When the solver selects the wrong class of solution (e.g., uses a brute-force search when an analytic solution is required, applies a sorting algorithm to an unsorted-order-required task, uses a banned library, or chooses a modeling approach that cannot address the problem structure).
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply when the method is valid but the execution of it is flawed — use B.2. Do not apply when the solver uses the right method but formats the output incorrectly — use B.1. Do not apply when the issue is merely that a better method exists but the chosen one is still acceptable.

codes.name: Checker_Harmful_Modification
codes.description: The checker modifies a draft and the modification causes net harm to the output — either by introducing a new constraint violation that was not present in the original draft, or by degrading the quality, correctness, or completeness of content that was already acceptable. The root failure is that the checker's intervention makes the output worse than it was before the checker acted. Covers both hard-constraint breaches introduced by edits and softer quality regressions.
codes.when_to_use: When a before/after comparison of the checker's edit shows that the post-edit output has a new problem (violation, error, omission, or quality degradation) not present in the pre-edit draft. Apply regardless of whether the checker also correctly fixed other issues in the same pass.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply when the checker fails to fix an existing problem but does not introduce any new one — use B.8. Do not apply when the checker produces a wrong verdict without editing the draft — use B.6. Do not apply when the draft was already non-compliant and the checker's edit leaves the same original violation intact without adding a new one.

codes.name: Checker_False_Compliance_Verdict
codes.description: The checker reviews a draft and produces a compliance verdict — whether as an explicit artifact (checklist, pass/fail summary, annotation list) or as an implicit approval (passing the draft through without flagging violations) — that is factually wrong. This covers both false positives (clearing a non-compliant draft) and false negatives (flagging a compliant draft as violating). The defining failure is that the checker's assessment of constraint compliance does not match reality.
codes.when_to_use: When the checker has performed a compliance review and its conclusion about whether the draft meets the task's constraints is demonstrably incorrect. Apply whether the verdict is stated explicitly or implied by the act of approving/rejecting the draft.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply when the checker correctly identifies a violation but then fails to fix it — use B.8. Do not apply when the checker edits the draft and introduces a new problem — use B.5. Do not apply when the checker's verdict is correct but its fix is inadequate.

codes.name: Checker_Identifies_But_Fails_To_Fix_Violation
codes.description: The checker correctly identifies one or more constraint violations or errors in the draft but produces a final output that still contains the identified violation — either leaving it entirely unaddressed or replacing it with a different problem. The checker's diagnostic work is sound; its corrective action is the failure.
codes.when_to_use: When evidence in the checker's output (explicit flagging, annotation, or commentary) confirms the checker detected a problem, yet the final emitted output still contains that problem or a direct substitute for it.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply when the checker never detected the violation in the first place — use B.6. Do not apply when the checker's fix attempt introduces a new, different problem — use B.5 (the identification credit does not prevent B.5 from applying to the new harm). Do not apply to the solver's original error that preceded checker involvement.

codes.name: Solver_Misinterprets_Task_Intent
codes.description: The solver fundamentally misunderstands what the task is asking and responds to the wrong problem — for example, treating a constraint-decorated prompt as a question about the constraints themselves, solving a related but different problem, or operating under a demonstrably false assumption about the task's goal.
codes.when_to_use: When the solver's response is internally coherent and potentially correct for some problem, but that problem is not the one actually posed. The mismatch must be at the level of task intent, not merely a minor misreading of a detail.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply when the solver addresses the right task but executes it incorrectly — use B.2. Do not apply when the solver uses the wrong method for the right task — use B.3. Do not apply to minor scope misreadings that do not redirect the entire response.

codes.name: Solver_Incomplete_Or_Shallow_Solution
codes.description: Apply this code when the solver's response (1) targets the correct topic, (2) contains no factually incorrect or misleading statements, BUT (3) is missing at least one element that can be identified by direct comparison against the prompt. The annotator must be able to quote or paraphrase the specific request from the prompt and then confirm it has no corresponding coverage in the response. Missing elements fall into two categories: EXPLICIT gaps — something the prompt directly asked for (e.g., 'provide three examples,' 'include installation steps,' 'list the pros and cons') that is entirely absent or present in insufficient quantity; or FUNCTIONAL gaps — a piece of information a reasonable person would need to act on the answer without external research, where that need is clearly implied by the prompt's context (e.g., a prompt asking how to deploy code receives an answer describing only the concept but omitting any commands or procedure). The omission must be nameable as a concrete noun or action: a step, an example, a condition, a formula, a section, a caveat — not a vague judgment that the answer 'could be deeper.'
codes.when_to_use: 1. The prompt explicitly requests N items, examples, steps, or sections and the response delivers fewer than N with no stated reason. 2. The prompt asks for a how-to or procedural answer and at least one step necessary to complete the procedure is absent. 3. The prompt requests a comparison or evaluation across multiple options and at least one named option receives no treatment. 4. The prompt specifies a required format or structural element (e.g., 'include a summary,' 'provide code,' 'add citations') and that element is completely absent. 5. The response answers part of a multi-part question and at least one sub-question is entirely unaddressed. In every case, the annotator should write a one-sentence statement of the form: 'The response does not include [specific element], which was [explicitly requested / necessary to act on the answer].'
codes.when_not_to_use: 1. The missing detail is a matter of depth or elaboration rather than a discrete, nameable element (use a 'shallow quality' code instead, if one exists). 2. The prompt is open-ended or opinion-seeking and no specific deliverables were listed — additional content would be nice but is not required. 3. The solver explicitly acknowledges the omission and explains why it was excluded (e.g., 'installation steps vary by OS; consult the official docs'). 4. The gap involves a factual error or misleading statement — that is a correctness failure, not an omission. 5. The annotator cannot point to a specific line or phrase in the prompt that implies the missing element is required. 6. The response is a clarifying question or a stated partial answer pending more user input.

codes.name: Constraint_Count_Mismatch
codes.description: The response contains the wrong number of required discrete elements — such as bullet points, paragraphs, keyword occurrences, sentences per paragraph, or words per sentence — where an explicit numeric requirement was stated.
codes.when_to_use: When the task specifies an exact or bounded count of structural elements and the response visibly has a different count. Applies to paragraph counts, bullet counts, keyword frequency, sentence counts, word counts per sentence, etc.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply when the count requirement is ambiguous or when the error is in the content of elements rather than their number. Do not apply when the violation is a formatting delimiter error rather than a count error.

codes.name: Differential_Equation_Or_Calculus_Procedure_Error
codes.description: The reasoning applies an incorrect calculus or differential equation procedure — such as wrong integration technique, incorrect boundary condition application, wrong differential operator, or invalid separation of variables — leading to an incorrect solution.
codes.when_to_use: When the task involves calculus or differential equations and the trace shows a procedural error in the mathematical method itself, such as integrating incorrectly, applying boundary conditions to the wrong expression, or choosing an inapplicable solution method.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply for arithmetic errors within an otherwise correct procedure (use C.10). Do not apply when the problem is purely algebraic with no calculus involved.

codes.name: Statistical_Or_Bayesian_Reasoning_Error
codes.description: The reasoning makes an error in statistical or probabilistic inference — misapplying Bayes' theorem, confusing prior/posterior/likelihood, using the wrong statistical test, or misinterpreting confidence intervals or p-values.
codes.when_to_use: When the task involves statistical inference or Bayesian reasoning and the trace contains a demonstrable logical error in the statistical argument, such as treating a posterior as a prior, inverting a conditional probability, or misidentifying what is being optimized.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply for arithmetic errors within correct statistical formulas (use C.10). Do not apply when the statistical approach is correct but the answer is imprecise due to rounding.

codes.name: Translation_Meaning_Distortion
codes.description: A natural language translation alters the meaning, tone, or key content of the source text — omitting important clauses, adding information not in the source, or producing a paraphrase that changes the factual or emotional content.
codes.when_to_use: When the task requires translation between languages and the output translation, when compared to the source text provided in the task, has substantively different meaning — not merely stylistic differences but semantic changes.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply for minor stylistic choices that preserve meaning. Do not apply when the response is in the wrong language (use C.9). Do not apply when the task is summarization rather than translation.

codes.name: Creative_Constraint_Non_Adherence
codes.description: In a creative or roleplay writing task, structural or thematic constraints specific to the creative task — such as genre, perspective, character consistency, narrative arc, or stylistic requirements — are violated while generic formatting constraints may be satisfied.
codes.when_to_use: When the task specifies creative writing requirements (e.g., 'write in first person', 'maintain the character's voice', 'follow a three-act structure') and the output violates those creative-domain constraints.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply to standard formatting constraints (paragraph count, keywords) that happen to appear in creative tasks — use C.1, C.2, or C.3 for those. Apply only when the violated constraint is specific to creative writing craft.

codes.name: Word_Uniqueness_Constraint_Violation
codes.description: The response repeats words when a 'no word may be repeated' or 'only unique words' constraint is in force, indicating failure to track lexical uniqueness across the full output.
codes.when_to_use: When the task explicitly requires every word to be unique and the response demonstrably reuses words (common function words like 'and', 'the', 'of', or content words).
codes.when_not_to_use: When no uniqueness constraint exists, or when apparent repetition is due to case variation treated as distinct tokens by the constraint.

codes.name: Sentence_Boundary_Word_Constraint_Failure
codes.description: The response fails to satisfy an explicit constraint on the first or last word of the response (or of individual sentences), such as requiring the response to begin or end with a specific word.
codes.when_to_use: When the task specifies 'the first word of your response should be X' or 'the last word should be Y' and the response begins or ends with a different word, including cases where punctuation or formatting elements precede/follow the required word.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the constraint concerns the first/last word of sections or bullet points rather than the overall response, or when the constraint is satisfied correctly.

codes.name: Language_Constraint_Violation
codes.description: The response contains content in a language other than what was explicitly required, either by mixing languages or using the wrong language entirely for the core response.
codes.when_to_use: When the task mandates a specific language (e.g., 'your entire response should be in Persian') and the response includes words, phrases, or passages in another language.
codes.when_not_to_use: When no language constraint exists, or when the non-compliant language appears only in quoted source material that was part of the original query rather than generated content.

codes.name: Paragraph_Structure_Constraint_Failure
codes.description: The response uses the wrong number of paragraphs, wrong paragraph delimiter, or incorrect paragraph ordering relative to explicit structural requirements (e.g., 'exactly 7 paragraphs separated by double newlines', 'paragraph 5 must start with word X').
codes.when_to_use: When a task specifies paragraph count, delimiter type (e.g., '\n\n', markdown divider '***'), or content rules for specific paragraphs and the response violates any of these.
codes.when_not_to_use: When paragraph structure is not explicitly constrained, or when the issue is purely about sentence count within paragraphs rather than paragraph-level structure.

codes.name: Keyword_Inclusion_Exclusion_Failure
codes.description: The response omits a required keyword, includes a prohibited keyword, or contains a required keyword the wrong number of times.
codes.when_to_use: When the task specifies a list of keywords to include or exclude and the response fails to comply — either a required keyword is absent, a forbidden keyword appears, or the required occurrence count is wrong.
codes.when_not_to_use: When keyword requirements are not stated, or when the keyword appears but in a clearly incidental/quoted context from the original prompt rather than the generated response.

codes.name: Adjacent_Letter_Constraint_Misapplication
codes.description: Incorrect application of the 'no two adjacent words may start with consecutive alphabet letters' rule, either by misidentifying which letter pairs are consecutive, failing to check all adjacent word pairs, or misunderstanding wrap-around alphabet adjacency.
codes.when_to_use: When the task requires the adjacent-letter constraint and the reasoning about which letters are consecutive is demonstrably wrong, or when the response/analysis fails to check all adjacent word pairs.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the constraint is not present, or when the error is a simple typo rather than a conceptual misapplication of the rule.

codes.name: Partial_Constraint_Satisfaction
codes.description: The response attempts to satisfy a constraint but does so incompletely — for example, including a keyword too few times, using the wrong delimiter for paragraph separation, or satisfying a positional requirement (first word of response) but not throughout (first word of each sentence).
codes.when_to_use: When evidence of an attempt to comply with a constraint is present in the response, but the compliance is incomplete or inconsistent across the full response.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply when the constraint is entirely absent (use C.2). Do not apply when the count is exactly correct but the constraint is a different type of violation.

codes.name: Formatting_Constraint_Applied_To_Wrong_Scope
codes.description: A formatting constraint that applies to the entire response (or to all sentences) is applied only to a subset — e.g., hyphen-connecting only some sentences, wrapping only some words in brackets, or applying capitalization only to certain paragraphs.
codes.when_to_use: When a constraint is stated as universal ('all sentences must be connected using hyphens', 'enclose every word in square brackets', 'entire response in all capitals') but the response applies it selectively or partially.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the constraint is explicitly scoped to a subset (e.g., 'only bullet points must be wrapped'), or when the partial application is due to system truncation.

codes.name: Post_Processing_Constraint_Regression
codes.description: A review/correction pass fixes one constraint violation but simultaneously breaks a constraint that was correctly satisfied in the prior draft, resulting in a final output that is no better or worse overall than the draft.
codes.when_to_use: When the trace shows a draft satisfying constraint X, a correction step targeting constraint Y, and the final output violating constraint X while satisfying Y — or when the correction changes a correct core answer to an incorrect one.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the correction step genuinely improves overall constraint compliance without introducing new violations, or when both draft and final output violate the same constraints.

codes.name: Refusal_Partial_Harmful_Content_Generation
codes.description: When refusing a harmful request, the response generates some portion of the harmful content before stopping, or satisfies some of the formatting constraints attached to the harmful core task, indicating incomplete refusal.
codes.when_to_use: When a task requests harmful content and the response begins generating it before refusing, or when the refusal message itself partially fulfills the harmful task (e.g., reproducing dangerous instructions then stopping).
codes.when_not_to_use: When the refusal is clean and complete with no harmful content generated, or when the content generated is clearly non-harmful framing/explanation rather than the requested harmful material.

codes.name: Incorrect_Core_Task_Answer
codes.description: The substantive answer to the core task is factually or computationally wrong, independent of whether formatting constraints are satisfied. This includes wrong mathematical results, incorrect translations, wrong factual claims, or logically flawed reasoning in the domain.
codes.when_to_use: When the domain answer itself — the math result, code logic, factual claim, or translation — contains a verifiable error detectable from the trace without solving the problem independently (e.g., an arithmetic step that contradicts a prior step, a formula applied to wrong variables, a translation that inverts meaning).
codes.when_not_to_use: When the error is purely in constraint compliance with the core answer being correct, or when determining correctness requires independent domain expertise not evident from the trace itself.

codes.name: Compliance_Verification_False_Positive
codes.description: A verification or self-check step incorrectly concludes that a constraint is satisfied when it is actually violated, or that the response is correct when it contains errors, failing to catch an existing problem.
codes.when_to_use: When the trace shows an explicit verification/checking step that reviews the response for constraint compliance or correctness and declares compliance or correctness, but inspection of the actual response reveals the declared constraint is violated or the answer is wrong.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the verification correctly identifies a violation (true positive detection), or when there is no explicit verification step in the trace.

codes.name: Conflicting_Constraint_Silent_Resolution
codes.description: Two or more stated constraints are mutually incompatible, but the response silently prioritizes one over another without acknowledging the conflict or explaining which constraint was sacrificed.
codes.when_to_use: When a task contains constraints that cannot simultaneously be satisfied (e.g., respond in under 2 words AND provide a technical explanation, or respond entirely in language X AND the first word must be an English word) and the response resolves the conflict without flagging it.
codes.when_not_to_use: When the constraints are compatible and can all be satisfied, or when the response explicitly acknowledges and explains the conflict.

codes.name: Capitalization_Constraint_Violation
codes.description: The response violates an explicit capitalization rule — such as all-lowercase, all-uppercase, or title-case requirements — by containing characters of the disallowed case, including in proper nouns, code identifiers, or headings.
codes.when_to_use: When the task specifies a capitalization rule (e.g., 'no capital letters', 'all uppercase', 'all lowercase') and the response contains characters that violate that rule.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply when the capitalization issue is inside a code block that is exempt from prose rules, and that exemption is clearly reasonable. Do not apply when the task does not specify a capitalization constraint.

codes.name: Core_Mathematical_Computation_Error
codes.description: The substantive mathematical result is incorrect due to an arithmetic or algebraic mistake — wrong formula application, sign error, incorrect order of operations, or miscalculation — independent of whether formatting constraints are satisfied.
codes.when_to_use: When the numeric or algebraic answer produced can be checked against the stated problem setup and is demonstrably wrong based on the reasoning shown in the trace (e.g., the trace shows intermediate steps that lead to an incorrect final value).
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply when the mathematical approach is correct and the answer is correct but constraints are violated. Do not apply when the mathematical error stems from a misunderstanding of the problem statement rather than computation (use C.11).

codes.name: Problem_Misinterpretation
codes.description: The reasoning proceeds correctly given a misread version of the problem — wrong quantity targeted, wrong constraint interpreted, wrong scope assumed — such that the approach is internally consistent but solves a different problem than stated.
codes.when_to_use: When the trace shows coherent reasoning that would produce a correct answer to a different problem than the one posed, indicating the problem statement was misread or a key condition was ignored or altered.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply when the problem statement itself is ambiguous. Do not apply when a specific arithmetic step is wrong but the problem was correctly understood (use C.10).

codes.name: Code_Logic_Error
codes.description: The translated or generated code contains a logical defect — wrong algorithm, incorrect loop bounds, missing edge case handling, wrong data structure operation — that would cause it to produce incorrect results or fail at runtime, independent of formatting constraints.
codes.when_to_use: When the code in the response can be inspected and a logical flaw is visible — such as an off-by-one in loop bounds, a missing base case, incorrect index arithmetic, or a semantic mismatch between the original and translated code.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply for minor stylistic code differences that do not affect correctness. Do not apply when the code logic is correct but formatting constraints around the code block are violated.

codes.name: Sentiment_Or_Classification_Error
codes.description: The response assigns an incorrect sentiment label, category, or classification to the input content, where the classification can be assessed against clear signals present in the source text provided in the task.
codes.when_to_use: When the task asks for sentiment analysis or classification and the label assigned contradicts clear linguistic signals in the provided source text (e.g., labeling an enthusiastic positive review as negative).
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply when the sentiment or classification is genuinely ambiguous. Do not apply when the correct label is given but the explanation is weak. Do not apply to factual question-answering errors (use C.13).

codes.name: Math_Symbol_Tokenization_Constraint_Error
codes.description: Formatting constraints that operate on words or word pairs (e.g., bigram wrapping, word count, letter-frequency count) are applied incorrectly because LaTeX math tokens, dollar signs, backslashes, or other symbolic markup are treated as words or letters, inflating or distorting the count.
codes.when_to_use: When the response contains mathematical notation (LaTeX, inline math) and a word-level or character-level constraint is evaluated in a way that counts math tokens as words or letters, leading to wrong compliance assessment.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply when the mathematical content uses no special markup. Do not apply when the word-count error is due to ordinary prose miscounting rather than math token confusion.

codes.name: Combinatorial_Or_Counting_Reasoning_Error
codes.description: The reasoning about a combinatorics, probability, or counting problem uses the wrong formula, applies the right formula to the wrong population, conflates combinations with permutations, or makes an error in case enumeration.
codes.when_to_use: When the task involves counting, probability, or combinatorial selection and the trace shows a reasoning path that applies incorrect combinatorial logic — such as using n! instead of C(n,k), double-counting cases, or missing cases in an enumeration.
codes.when_not_to_use: Do not apply for simple arithmetic errors in otherwise correct combinatorial reasoning (use C.10). Do not apply when the task is not combinatorial in nature.
